scene-u01.name: Pattern Recognition Week 3 KP11 MSE and Posterior Probability (expert-first, English)

p01-indicator-title.name: p01-indicator-title
p01-indicator-title.text: Turn classes into 0/1 and "average" gets a meaning: it equals the posterior probability

p01-indicator-ctx.name: p01-indicator-ctx
p01-indicator-ctx.text: Three classes (ω₁, ω₂, ω₃). Each sample is a "single 1" vector $\mathbf y$: the column of its class is 1 and the others 0.

p01-indicator-src.name: p01-indicator-src
p01-indicator-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture §1: $y_i=\mathbf 1\{\omega=\omega_i\}$, $E[y_i\mid\mathbf x]=1\cdot p_i+0\cdot(1-p_i)=p_i(\mathbf x)$; the three probabilities $0.5,0.3,0.2$ at a fixed input are this page's illustration.

p01-indicator-c0.name: p01-indicator-c0
p01-indicator-c0.text: Fix the same input $\mathbf x$: when the observed sample class differs, the target vector differs.

p01-indicator-bl.name: p01-indicator-bl
p01-indicator-bl.text: At this $\mathbf x$, the posterior probabilities of the three classes $p_i=P(\omega_i\mid\mathbf x)$:

p01-indicator-c1.name: p01-indicator-c1
p01-indicator-c1.text: Each time we see this $\mathbf x$, $y_i$ is 1 with chance $p_i$ and 0 with chance $1-p_i$.

p01-indicator-c2.name: p01-indicator-c2
p01-indicator-c2.text: On average: $E[y_i\mid\mathbf x]=1\cdot p_i+0\cdot(1-p_i)=p_i(\mathbf x)$. The conditional mean is the posterior probability, with no Gaussian assumption and no need to estimate each class's density first.

p01-indicator-c3.name: p01-indicator-c3
p01-indicator-c3.text: So KP10's conclusion applies directly: under squared loss the best $g_i(\mathbf x)$ is $E[y_i\mid\mathbf x]=P(\omega_i\mid\mathbf x)$. Learning "the mean of 0/1" means learning the posterior probability.

p02-eight-two-title.name: p02-eight-two-title
p02-eight-two-title.text: 10 records: 8 are 1 and 2 are 0. What guess minimizes the squared loss?

p02-eight-two-ctx.name: p02-eight-two-ctx
p02-eight-two-ctx.text: Source: at input $x_0=2$, $p_1(x_0)=0.8$, illustrated with 10 records (8 labeled 1, 2 labeled 0).

p02-eight-two-src.name: p02-eight-two-src
p02-eight-two-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture §3: the sample proportion $8/10$ happens to equal the source's assumed population probability; in general a sampled proportion is only an estimate and does not prove the true probability is $0.8$.

p02-eight-two-c0.name: p02-eight-two-c0
p02-eight-two-c0.text: The whole bar represents 10 records. If we may report one number $g$, what is best? What are the squared losses of reporting $0.8$ and of reporting $1$?

p02-eight-two-c1.name: p02-eight-two-c1
p02-eight-two-c1.text: Average: $\bar y=\dfrac{8(1)+2(0)}{10}=0.8$. The sample proportion equals the assumed population probability $0.8$.

p02-eight-two-c4.name: p02-eight-two-c4
p02-eight-two-c4.text: Reporting $1$ pays $0.04=(1-0.8)^2$ more. The goal is not to output the right class for every record but to reflect "under the same conditions the class is uncertain": the two 0s really do happen.

p03-parabola-title.name: p03-parabola-title
p03-parabola-title.text: Plot "what to report" against "squared loss": the bottom is at g = p, with height p(1−p)

p03-parabola-src.name: p03-parabola-src
p03-parabola-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture §2: $E[(g_i-y_i)^2\mid\mathbf x]=(g_i-p_i)^2+p_i(1-p_i)$, the second term being the conditional variance of a 0/1 variable; numbers use $p=0.8$, recomputed by build_kp11_en.py.

p03-parabola-c0.name: p03-parabola-c0
p03-parabola-c0.text: What shape does the loss take as $g$ varies? Where is the lowest point and how high is it?

p03-parabola-c1.name: p03-parabola-c1
p03-parabola-c1.text: Blue bowl: $(g-0.8)^2+0.16$. The first term $(g-p)^2$ varies with $g$; the second is a constant.

p03-parabola-c2.name: p03-parabola-c2
p03-parabola-c2.text: Bottom $g=p=0.8$: loss $0.16=p(1-p)$. This is the class's own uncertainty, which no one can remove.

p03-parabola-c3.name: p03-parabola-c3
p03-parabola-c3.text: Report $1$: $0.16+(0.2)^2=0.2$. Report $0.5$: $0.16+(0.3)^2=0.25$. The farther from the probability, the more paid is $(g-p)^2$.

p03-parabola-c4.name: p03-parabola-c4
p03-parabola-c4.text: So the theoretical target of squared loss is the posterior probability $p$, not a "yes/no" label.

p04-multiclass-title.name: p04-multiclass-title
p04-multiclass-title.text: Multiclass: total squared loss = approximation term + fixed term; a linear model lowers only the former

p04-multiclass-ctx.name: p04-multiclass-ctx
p04-multiclass-ctx.text: Sum over all classes: $J=E\bigl[\sum_i(g_i-p_i)^2\bigr]+E\bigl[\sum_ip_i(1-p_i)\bigr]$. Take the three-class probabilities $(0.5,0.3,0.2)$.

p04-multiclass-src.name: p04-multiclass-src
p04-multiclass-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture §2 total formula and [supplement]: fixed term $=E[1-\sum_ip_i^2]$; $(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ and the prediction $(0.6,0.3,0.1)$ are this page's illustration.

p04-multiclass-c0.name: p04-multiclass-c0
p04-multiclass-c0.text: The fixed term $\sum p_i(1-p_i)$ is independent of the model; the approximation term $\sum(g_i-p_i)^2$ is the one the model decides. What are they?

p04-multiclass-sa.name: p04-multiclass-sa
p04-multiclass-sa.text: The prediction exactly equals the probabilities: $g=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$

p04-multiclass-c1.name: p04-multiclass-c1
p04-multiclass-c1.text: First bar: approximation term $0$, total loss $=0.62$. This is a lower bound no predictor can go below (an unrestricted function can reach it).

p04-multiclass-c2.name: p04-multiclass-c2
p04-multiclass-c2.text: Second bar: approximation term $(0.1)^2+0+(0.1)^2=0.02$ (short red segment), total loss $0.64$. The larger the bias, the longer the red segment.

p04-multiclass-c3.name: p04-multiclass-c3
p04-multiclass-c3.text: If the function is unrestricted the approximation term can fall to 0; if only linear functions are allowed, we look for the one nearest the posterior probability within the linear family. The data's class uncertainty still leaves squared loss, so "loss above 0" does not mean the model is bad.

p05-fit-title.name: p05-fit-title
p05-fit-title.text: The true posterior probability is an S-shaped curve; a line can only approximate it, and may exceed 1

p05-fit-ctx.name: p05-fit-ctx
p05-fit-ctx.text: Supplementary model: $p_1(x)=\sigma(\ln4+x-2)$, $p_1(2)=0.8$; inputs are the integers $-2\ldots6$, equally likely.

p05-fit-src.name: p05-fit-src
p05-fit-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture §4 [supplementary model]: the best linear approximation on 9 points $g_1(x)=0.128768669x+0.392144754$; recomputed by build_kp11_en.py here (about 1.164757 at $x=6$, not a valid probability).

p05-fit-c0.name: p05-fit-c0
p05-fit-c0.text: See the range of probabilities first: only between 0 and 1 (red dashed). What does the true posterior look like? Can a line fit it?

p05-fit-c1.name: p05-fit-c1
p05-fit-c1.text: The blue S-shaped curve is the posterior probability, and the three blue points mark the posterior at x=−2, 2, 6. The probability slowly rises to 1 but never exceeds it.

p05-fit-c2.name: p05-fit-c2
p05-fit-c2.text: Orange is the best linear approximation on 9 points $g_1=0.128769x+0.392145$: along the middle of the curve, missing both ends.

p05-fit-c3.name: p05-fit-c3
p05-fit-c3.text: At $x=6$: the line gives $1.164757>1$, not a valid probability (true probability $0.995$). The left end $x=-2$ is also too high ($0.135$ versus the true $0.068$).

p05-fit-c4.name: p05-fit-c4
p05-fit-c4.text: One line serves all inputs, so it may fail to fit the true probability curve, and its output may even leave $[0,1]$.

p06-coding-title.name: p06-coding-title
p06-coding-title.text: A score is not a calibrated probability: clipping only fixes the range, and a change of coding needs conversion

p06-coding-ctx.name: p06-coding-ctx
p06-coding-ctx.text: For the same probability $p=0.8$ the conditional mean differs under different codings; and a score outside the range is not fixed by just clipping.

p06-coding-src.name: p06-coding-src
p06-coding-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture §5: clipping only repairs the range and does not guarantee calibration; the 0.5 threshold must match the decision and its costs; the conditional mean of the $-1/+1$ coding is $2p_1-1$.

p06-coding-c0.name: p06-coding-c0
p06-coding-c0.text: The two number lines below are two representations of the same probability. What is 0.8 in the $-1/+1$ coding?

p06-coding-c1.name: p06-coding-c1
p06-coding-c1.text: $p=0.8\ \Rightarrow\ 2p-1=0.6$. The same squared-loss target needs different conversions under different codings.

p06-coding-c2.name: p06-coding-c2
p06-coding-c2.text: The score $1.165$ leaves $[0,1]$ (red point). Clipping to 1 only fixes the range.

p06-coding-c3.name: p06-coding-c3
p06-coding-c3.text: A clipped 1 still need not equal the true frequency (no calibration); the binary $0.5$ threshold also depends on the decision and its costs and is not a fixed answer to every risk problem. First check the range, then check whether predicted probabilities match actual frequencies.

p07-practice-title.name: p07-practice-title
p07-practice-title.text: Practice: p₁(x_A) = 0.7: what are the expected squared losses of predicting 0.7 and of predicting 1?

p07-practice-ctx.name: p07-practice-ctx
p07-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: use "fixed term + squared deviation"; no need to assume a feature density. Press Next when done.

p07-practice-src.name: p07-practice-src
p07-practice-src.text: Source: KP11 lecture practice; answer computed by build_kp11_en.py and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp11.py.

p07-practice-q.name: p07-practice-q
p07-practice-q.text: (a) Expected squared loss of predicting $0.7$? (b) Expected squared loss of predicting $1$? (c) The difference?

p07-practice-a3.name: p07-practice-a3
p07-practice-a3.text: (c) Reporting $1$ pays $(1-0.7)^2=0.09$ more than reporting $0.7$. The fixed term $0.21$ is the same for both; only the deviation term differs.

p08-summary-title.name: p08-summary-title
p08-summary-title.text: Summary: squared loss targets the posterior probability; a line only approximates it and may leave [0,1]

p08-summary-ctx.name: p08-summary-ctx
p08-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the S-shaped curve and the line; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p08-summary-e0.name: p08-summary-e0
p08-summary-e0.text: 0/1 (single 1) coding: $E[y_i\mid\mathbf x]=p_i(\mathbf x)$, no Gaussian assumption needed

p08-summary-e2.name: p08-summary-e2
p08-summary-e2.text: Multiclass: approximation term (the model can lower it) + fixed term $1-\sum p_i^2$ (it cannot)

p08-summary-e3.name: p08-summary-e3
p08-summary-e3.text: A linear score is only an approximation and may leave $[0,1]$; clipping is not calibration; $-1/+1$ coding needs the conversion $2p-1$

p08-summary-e4.name: p08-summary-e4
p08-summary-e4.text: Open question: can we guarantee valid probabilities from the start? Next KP: bias and variance, then logistic regression
